clue.text: Throw in a few more chips!

definitions.text: Throw in a few more chips!

parts.words: Throw in a few more chips!
parts.note: read literally this is a poker player adding chips to the pile being bet on, which is also the idiom for making a deal more tempting

explanation.surface: A gambler is urged to put more chips on the table.
explanation.walkthrough: In poker the chips being bet sit in the middle of the table; adding to them makes winning the hand more rewarding, and the phrase is used for any extra inducement.
explanation.definitionFit: The idiom means adding an inducement, taken from poker, where the chips in the middle are what a winning hand collects.

clue.text: See 27 across
Get on board, because 10 is confused over the downpour.

indicators.note: in a down clue, over places the first piece above the second
confused tells us the letters of ten are jumbled

parts.note: the number ten, written as a word
a downpour is heavy rain

explanation.surface: A passenger hurries aboard, flustered by the rain.
explanation.walkthrough: The 10 is not a cross-reference to another clue; it is just the number written as a word, which 'confused' scrambles to ENT. Being a down clue, 'over' means ENT sits above the rain.
explanation.definitionFit: To entrain is to board a train, the railway counterpart of embark.

clue.text: A choice offering around the end of October.

definitions.text: A choice offering around the end of October.

parts.words: A choice offering around the end of October.
parts.note: Halloween falls on 31 October, when children at the door offer the householder a choice: a treat, or a prank played on them

explanation.surface: Something on offer as a choice in late October.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Offering a choice' is meant literally: the children's call at the door gives two options.
explanation.definitionFit: The Halloween doorstep call offers two alternatives, a prank or a sweet, on the last day of October.

clue.text: Mailer's French conquerors.

definitions.meaning: first meaning: belonging to Norman Mailer, the American novelist
second meaning: the ... from northern France who conquered England in 1066

explanation.walkthrough: Mailer's first name is Norman, so 'Mailer's' gives NORMAN'S; with the apostrophe dropped it is also the plural people.
explanation.definitionFit: The Normans were the people of Normandy, whose duke William won the Battle of Hastings and took the English throne.

clue.text: See 3 down
Possibly a fine result from books being so!

definitions.text: Possibly a fine result from books being so!

parts.words: Possibly a fine result from books being so!
parts.note: library books returned late earn the borrower a small penalty charge

explanation.walkthrough: A 'fine result' sounds like praise for something done well, but the fine is the late charge a library imposes.
explanation.definitionFit: Overdue describes a library book kept past its return date, which is what earns the penalty.

clue.text: One from Baghdad was famous–or infamous.

definitions.text: One from Baghdad was famous–or infamous.

parts.words: One from Baghdad was famous–or infamous.
parts.note: a classic film of 1924, remade in 1940, is named for a famous Baghdad robber, and anyone in that trade is infamous

explanation.walkthrough: The 'famous' one from Baghdad is the title character of the classic film; 'or infamous' adds that any such person is a villain.
explanation.definitionFit: A thief is a robber, someone known for wrongdoing rather than celebrated, which is why 'infamous' fits too.

clue.text: How we are told certain truths may be, self-started.

definitions.text: How we are told certain truths may be, self-started.

parts.words: How we are told certain truths may be, self-started.
parts.note: the US Declaration of Independence says it holds certain truths in a particular way, and the clue asks for that phrase with its opening self removed

explanation.walkthrough: The Declaration of Independence says 'We hold these truths to be self-evident'; 'self-started' tells you the answer is what follows SELF.
explanation.definitionFit: Evident means plainly true or obvious, the sense the Declaration's phrase self-evident relies on.

clue.text: Possibly a duet, say–with the middle of the week approaching!

definitions.text: Possibly a duet, say–with the middle of the week approaching!

parts.words: Possibly a duet, say–with the middle of the week approaching!
parts.note: a duet is a twos' performance, and 'two's day' sounds like the day that comes just before midweek Wednesday

explanation.walkthrough: A duet is for two, so it is a 'two's day' by pun; the day so pronounced comes right before Wednesday, the middle of the week.
explanation.definitionFit: Tuesday is the weekday immediately preceding Wednesday, so midweek is approaching on it.

clue.text: Return one of the colors to the row which is sharper!

indicators.note: Return asks for the colour word to be sent back the way it came, read from right to left

parts.note: tan is a light brown colour
a tier is a row, as of seats

explanation.surface: A painter sends a colour back to a row of others to make the effect sharper.
explanation.walkthrough: The definition is sharper as in smartly dressed, not keener. 'Return' applies only to the colour, giving NAT, not to the row.
explanation.definitionFit: Nattier means smarter or more stylish in dress, which is one sense of sharper.

clue.text: Fancy building this!

parts.note: an imposing, elaborate structure is called by this grand word

explanation.walkthrough: 'Fancy' reads like an exclamation ('fancy that!') but is an adjective: the answer is a grand building.
explanation.definitionFit: An edifice is a large, imposing structure, the kind of grand building the clue exclaims over.

clue.text: What the detective and the shortstop might be expected to do and meet the answer.

definitions.text: What the detective and the shortstop might be expected to do and meet the answer.

parts.words: What the detective and the shortstop might be expected to do and meet the answer.
parts.note: the answer with 'meet' after it names an athletics competition

explanation.walkthrough: The two jobs give the two halves: a detective tracks and a shortstop, a baseball infielder, fields. 'Meet the answer' says the answer plus 'meet' is a sporting event.
explanation.definitionFit: Track and field is the American name for athletics; its competitions are called meets.

clue.text: See 11
See 11
They don't offer much time for what started the scale long ago to be in the pits, but they might be taken from the meeting.

indicators.note: to be in tells us the old note goes inside the word for the pits

parts.note: pits dug for coal or ore are mines

parts.words: what started the scale long ago
parts.note: ut was the medieval name for the first note of the scale, later replaced by do

explanation.surface: A sly dig at short meetings whose records are kept by a secretary.
explanation.walkthrough: UT is the old name for the first note of the sol-fa scale, now called do; 'to be in' puts it inside the pits. The last part, 'they might be taken from the meeting', is a second, joking definition: a meeting's written record.
explanation.definitionFit: A minute is sixty seconds, a short span of time; minutes are also the written record taken at a meeting.

clue.text: See 1 across
Get me back on track, with your beginning to have a vicarious experience.

indicators.note: on joins the turned word to the track word, which follows it
back means the little word me is read the other way round

parts.note: a track is a path

indicators.note: beginning means only the first letter of your is taken

parts.note: the word whose first letter is used

explanation.surface: Someone asks to be set back on the right path and to share another's experience.
explanation.walkthrough: 'back' reverses the little word me to EM, 'on' sets the track after it, and 'beginning' takes only the opening letter of 'your' to close the word.
explanation.definitionFit: Empathy is feeling what another person feels, sharing their experience second-hand as if it were one's own.

clue.text: See 1 across
One might hope such are well oiled, unless they typify those who praise fulsomely.

definitions.text: One might hope such are well oiled
definitions.meaning: first meaning: oil wells that spout freely, which a prospector hopes to strike

definitions.text: they typify those who praise fulsomely
definitions.meaning: second meaning: people who talk effusively, pouring out praise

explanation.walkthrough: 'Well oiled' looks like slang for drunk but means oil wells; 'unless' only joins the two meanings.
explanation.definitionFit: A gusher is both an oil well that flows without pumping and a person who speaks with excessive enthusiasm.

clue.text: Gets set about what the ship may say before its name, being set inside–and they may improve the fit.

indicators.note: set about tells us the word gets is placed around the ship letters
being set inside confirms the ship's letters go within the other word

parts.note: taken as written

parts.words: what the ship may say before its name
parts.note: USS, United States Ship, is the prefix to a US Navy vessel's name, as in USS Enterprise

explanation.surface: Instructions for fitting out a ship's name, which then turn into tailoring.
explanation.walkthrough: United States Navy vessels carry a three-letter prefix before their names, as in 'Enterprise'. 'set about' and 'being set inside' both say the same thing: that prefix goes within 'Gets'.
explanation.definitionFit: Gussets are triangular pieces of fabric sewn into a garment to give it more room or strength.

clue.text: A second-year student starts to sit improperly, being somewhat of a thinker.

indicators.note: starts tells us the student comes first in the answer

parts.note: soph is short for sophomore, the American name for a second-year student

indicators.note: improperly says the letters of sit are put in the wrong order

explanation.surface: A sophomore slouches in class and fancies themself a philosopher.
explanation.walkthrough: In American schools and colleges a second-year student is a sophomore, shortened in the usual way. 'starts' puts the student at the front, and 'improperly' scrambles 'sit' into IST after it.
explanation.definitionFit: A sophist is a clever arguer, a philosopher of a kind, though one more concerned with persuasion than truth.

clue.text: Frequently found between two points, and makes things less hard.

indicators.note: found between places the word for frequently inside the two compass letters

parts.note: two compass points, here both S for south
frequently means often

explanation.surface: Something often turns up between two points and eases things.
explanation.walkthrough: Compass points are a crossword stock: here both are south, and 'found between' puts the word for frequently between them.
explanation.definitionFit: To soften something is to make it less hard, whether butter or a blow.

clue.text: You expect the wine not to be what the garden should be.

definitions.text: You expect the wine not to be
definitions.meaning: first meaning: diluted, which nobody wants their wine to be
second meaning: given water, as plants need

explanation.walkthrough: The same word is a complaint about wine and a duty in the garden.
explanation.definitionFit: Watered describes wine thinned with water and also plants that have been given water to drink.

clue.text: Wild talk about fighting? Vouch for it!

indicators.note: about here means the wild talk concerns the fighting, so the fighting comes first

parts.note: fighting between nations is war
to rant is to talk wildly

explanation.surface: A soldier's wild boasting about combat, with a challenge to back it up.
explanation.walkthrough: Read 'wild talk about fighting' as a WAR RANT: a rant on the subject of war.
explanation.definitionFit: To warrant something is to guarantee it, to stand behind it as true.

clue.text: They might be typified by the Ponderosa for some people, being operated by the revolutionary to the South.

definitions.text: They might be typified by the Ponderosa for some people

parts.note: a business that someone operated, they ran
Che Guevara is the archetypal revolutionary
S is the compass abbreviation for south

explanation.surface: A famous TV homestead, operated by a guerrilla in the south.
explanation.walkthrough: The Ponderosa was the Cartwright family's spread in the American TV western Bonanza, so it is the model ranch for many viewers.
explanation.definitionFit: Ranches are large farms for raising cattle; the Ponderosa of Bonanza is the best-known example on television.

clue.text: Desired wrongly to show what the mocker does.

indicators.note: wrongly says the letters of desired are put in a different order

explanation.surface: Wanting something the wrong way earns a mocker's scorn.
explanation.walkthrough: 'wrongly' rearranges the seven letters of 'Desired', and 'to show' only links them to the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: To deride is to ridicule, the scornful laughter a mocker directs at someone.

clue.text: High fliers that could do lots of damage, although excellent for your hair!

definitions.text: High fliers that could do lots of damage

parts.note: super means excellent
tresses are long locks of hair

explanation.surface: A shampoo advert's boast that sounds like a review of bombers.
explanation.walkthrough: The Superfortress was the American B-29 bomber of the Second World War; 'although' only joins the two parts.
explanation.definitionFit: The B-29 Superfortress was a high-altitude heavy bomber, capable of enormous destruction.

clue.text: You can't say this girl doesn't have a hoard made up!

indicators.note: made up means the letters are assembled into a new word

explanation.surface: A girl who certainly has a stash made up.
explanation.walkthrough: 'made up' says the letters of 'hoard' are rearranged into her name, which is the joke: you cannot deny she has one.
explanation.definitionFit: Rhoda is a female first name, so it can stand for a particular girl.

clue.text: See 24
That special space of yours.

parts.note: the most private room of a person, where no visitor is allowed

explanation.walkthrough: A sanctum is a holy place; the full phrase is used for a person's most private retreat.
explanation.definitionFit: An inner sanctum is a private room or refuge reserved for oneself and very few others.

clue.text: Kinda stupid, in a Northeast way.

parts.note: NE is the compass abbreviation for northeast

explanation.surface: A northeasterner's way of talking dismissed as a bit dim.
explanation.walkthrough: The clue words string together almost as they stand: IN, A, NE.
explanation.definitionFit: Inane means silly or senseless, a close relation of stupid.

clue.text: One typical of a whole class, with a slice of pie given to me.

definitions.text: One typical of a whole class

indicators.note: given tells us the pie is handed over, followed by to me
slice of tells us the pie is cut up, its letters rearranged

explanation.surface: Someone is handed a slice of pie as the class example.
explanation.walkthrough: 'slice of' cuts PIE into EPI, and 'given' passes it TO ME.
explanation.definitionFit: An epitome is the perfect example of a type, the one that sums up the whole class.

clue.text: Has proven wrong when sleeping around–being somewhat embarrassed.

indicators.note: around says the sleeping word goes round the reworked letters

parts.note: someone sleeping is abed, in bed

indicators.note: proven wrong signals that the letters of has are wrong as they stand and must be rearranged

explanation.surface: Someone caught out in bed, red-faced.
explanation.walkthrough: 'proven wrong' scrambles 'Has' into ASH, and 'around' wraps the word for sleeping (in bed) about it; 'when' and 'being' are only links.
explanation.definitionFit: Abashed means embarrassed or disconcerted, made to feel ashamed.

clue.text: Old Persian monarchs took the chair with what many a modern entertainer does.

parts.note: someone who took a chair sat down

parts.words: what many a modern entertainer does
parts.note: rap is a popular music form, so a rapper raps

explanation.surface: Ancient rulers on thrones next to modern performers on stage.
explanation.walkthrough: 'took the chair' means sat down, not chaired a meeting.
explanation.definitionFit: Satraps were the provincial governors of the ancient Persian empire, rulers of their own regions.

clue.text: See 24
